title: What a walkdown is for
task: Learn a compartment in the order the facts depend on each other.
scene: Chief Petty Officer Dario Ferro walks you into the forward space and tells you to learn it. Kit down both sides. A hose reel on the wall. Two ways out.
assumes: a submarine is split into compartments that can be sealed off from each other
takeaway: A compartment is a sealed box first, and everything else you learn about it hangs off that.
why: A submarine survives by being divided. The sealed boundary matters first. Ninety metres down it is what keeps a flooded compartment from becoming a flooded boat. The ways out come next, and they have to be tried rather than assumed. Then look for what could start a casualty in here: sea pipes, cables, stores. Only then does the kit mean anything. A locker is the right locker once you know what this space can do to you.

cards: Find where the sealed boundary runs, because it decides whose flood this is.
Prove both hatches out of here still open, by trying them.
Find what in here could start a fire or a flood — sea pipes, cables, stores.
Judge whether the kit stowed here could fight one.
rebuttals: The boundary first. It is what makes this a space of its own, and everything else is about what happens inside it.
Both ways out second, and proved. A hatch nobody has tried is not a way out.
What could start a casualty third. You cannot judge the kit until you know the threat.
Whether this space can fight it, last. That is a judgement about the first three.

title: Every fitting is an argument
task: Match each fitting to what it is there to do.
scene: Chief Machinist's Mate Jun Haruki stops at four fittings on one wall and asks what each is for. None has a label, only a number. He steps back from the valves and waits.
assumes: water pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every ten metres of depth
takeaway: What a fitting is for is decided by what is on the other side of it.
why: A fitting makes sense once you join its shape to what lies behind it. A wheel valve through the hull may have the sea behind it, at pressure. A manifold at head height can feed breathing air. A strapped locker can hold props and plugs. A hose reel can put water on a fire. The point is not to learn four shapes. It is to work out what a thing does from where it sits.

scenarios: A wheel valve on a pipe that runs through the hull.
A manifold at head height with quick-connect couplings.
A strapped steel locker with a quick-release catch.
A folded hose on a reel, beside a small shut-off valve.
choices: Open it ninety metres down and the sea comes in at ten atmospheres.
It gives people air to breathe before a space is fit to enter.
It holds the props and plugs this compartment fights with.
It puts water on a fire, once the circuit is proved dead.
rebuttals: A wheel valve on a pipe through the hull is the one with the ocean behind it. Depth decides what comes through.
Quick-connect couplings at head height are breathing air. A supply for people, not for a machine.
A strapped locker with a quick-release catch holds what a crew shores and plugs with.
A folded hose on a reel is firefighting water, and it goes on after the circuit is proved dead.

title: The trip back without a waypoint
task: Learn the route, rebuild it without labels, then recover when one door is shut.
scene: Lieutenant Imani Sowande, the navigator, sends you aft with a sealed note. On the way back one door will be shut and the marker lights off. You have walked it once, with labels.
assumes: a submarine is divided into named compartments
a route can be remembered as a list of places
takeaway: A route remembered as places survives an interruption. A count of turns does not.
question: Run the route from memory. After the shut door, use the landmark to work out where the detour has put you.
why: A count works only while nothing interrupts it. A turn list fails after one extra turn. A route made of places is different, because each compartment is a fresh reference point. Get diverted and you name the space you are standing in. Then you rejoin the list from there. The useful question is not how many steps have gone by. It is which reference you can still trust.
answerText: The order runs Control, Radio, Crew Mess, Berthing, Auxiliary Machinery, Engine Room, Machinery Control. The shut door sends you round. You come back in at Auxiliary Machinery. Carry on from there.

title: Four traces, one of them ours
task: Match each trace to what is making it.
scene: Four traces sit on the display while the watch calls them out. The boat slowed four minutes ago and one trace changed with it. Petty Officer Nils Rask, the sonar supervisor, wants each one named.
assumes: passive sonar only listens; it sends nothing out
takeaway: A sound that changes when the boat changes belongs to the boat.
why: Every trace here has more than one clue on it. A sound that follows our own speed is being made aboard. A narrow tone that drifts slowly in direction fits machinery on another ship holding a course. Short chirps that vanish fit something alive better than a hull. And a direction that barely moves while the sound grows louder is the one to say out loud. You name a trace by combining its clues, not by picking the loudest.

scenarios: A steady hiss that rises and falls with our own speed.
A narrow tone at one pitch, drifting slowly in direction.
Short chirps with no drift at all, gone within a minute.
Two tones an octave apart, direction barely moving, growing louder.
choices: It is being made aboard this boat.
Machinery on a ship holding a steady course.
Something alive, passing through.
Something on a course that closes with ours.
rebuttals: A sound that follows our own throttle is ours. Nothing out in the water knows what our engine is doing.
A narrow tone at one pitch, drifting slowly, is machinery on a ship that is holding its course.
Short chirps that vanish in a minute do not behave the way a hull has to. That is life, not a contact.
Direction holding still while the sound grows louder is the pattern that matters. Say that one out loud.

title: The trace that will not resolve
task: Say which explanation fits every reading, not only the loudest one.
scene: The fourth trace is faint. It has held nearly the same direction for eleven minutes, and it shows no tone at all on the narrow display. The boat has not changed speed or depth since it appeared.
assumes: sound bends when it crosses water at a different temperature
a narrow display looks for steady tones, and a broad one measures sound of every pitch at once
takeaway: Bending can make a sound faint. It cannot pick out and remove that sound's tones.
question: Which explanation fits every reading here?
why: The broad display measures sound of every pitch at once. The narrow one hunts for steady tones. A layer of warmer water can bend a path and make a far-off source arrive faint. It cannot reach in and strip that source's tones away. So faintness and missing tones are two separate clues. The layer explains the first. The second says no tone is loud enough to show. Eleven minutes says it is not a flicker.

choices: Something outside, arriving faint.
Our own machinery, sounding outboard.
Something alive, holding station.
A flicker in the software.
Ordinary background noise, nothing more.
choiceMechanisms: A far-off source can arrive faint after bending, with no tone loud enough to show.
Anything aboard usually changes when our own machinery changes.
Something alive rarely holds one direction for eleven minutes.
Software drawing lines from nothing would not carry real sound energy.
Sound that keeps coming from one direction is not random background.
rebuttals: Nothing aboard changed when the trace appeared, so our own noise does not fit the timing.
Something alive is possible, and eleven minutes on nearly one direction fits it badly.
The broad display is receiving real sound. The question is what made it, not whether it was drawn from nothing.
Sound that keeps coming from one direction is evidence, and evidence needs an explanation.
text.headline: A faint trace has held the same direction for eleven minutes and shows no tone at all.

title: The bearing that does not move
task: Say what a steady bearing and a rising level mean together.
scene: The contact has stayed within half a degree of the same bearing for six minutes. It gets louder on every sweep. The boat is still making eight knots, and the channel narrows ahead.
assumes: passive sonar gives a direction and no distance at all
takeaway: A bearing that holds while the sound grows is a closing course, not a quiet one.
question: What do a steady bearing and a rising level tell you together?
why: A bearing is a direction, not a distance. If the direction holds while the sound grows louder, the two tracks are not sliding safely past each other. That is what a closing course looks like from a boat with no range. The steady bearing alone would not prove it. The rising level alone would not either. Together they rule out the comfortable answer, and that is enough to act on.

choices: We are closing with it, and the range is shrinking.
It has stopped, since its bearing is not changing.
It is drawing away, and the noise is rising for some other reason.
Nothing at all, until somebody has a range.
rebuttals: A contact that had stopped would slide in bearing as we went past it.
Something drawing away gets quieter, not louder.
Waiting for a range throws away the six minutes the geometry just handed you.

title: How far the water has carried us
task: Work out how far the current could have moved the boat since the last fix.
scene: The last trusted fix was three and a half hours ago. The current here runs about half a knot. Nobody has put it on the plot, because nobody has measured it.
assumes: the log measures speed through the water, not speed over the ground
takeaway: Dead reckoning tells you where you would be if nothing had pushed you.
question: How far could the boat be from where the plot says it is?
why: Between fixes the boat carries its position forward from the last known point, using course, speed and time. That is dead reckoning. The water moves as well. A current can carry the whole boat sideways, and it never shows up in the speed through the water. Half a knot for three and a half hours is nearly two sea miles. The error grows every hour nobody measures it. This is the plot the boat enters the narrows on.

estimate.prompt: The current has been running about half a knot since the last trusted fix.
estimate.question: How far could the boat be from where the plot says it is?
estimate.relationship: Distance = speed × time. A knot is one sea mile in an hour.
estimate.explanation: The rate here is the water, not the boat. Our own speed is already drawn on the plot, so it is not part of the error.
estimate.solution: Half a knot for three and a half hours is nearly two sea miles nobody has drawn.

title: Two displays, one source
task: Say what the agreement between the two navigation displays is worth.
scene: The two navigation displays agree to within a hundred yards. The sounder's ping comes back in 0.120 seconds. The chart says one hundred and two metres here. The last trusted fix was three and a half hours ago.
assumes: an echo time covers the trip down and the trip back
two displays fed by one source can be wrong in the same way
takeaway: Agreement is only a check when the second measurement could have failed differently.
question: What can you say from these readings, before the banked water?
why: The sounder measures a time. Sound goes down and comes back at about fifteen hundred metres a second, so 0.120 seconds is one hundred and eighty metres of travelling. The bottom is half of that: ninety metres. The chart says one hundred and two, so something is wrong by twelve. The two displays cannot settle it, because both repeat one source. That is one measurement shown twice. The sounder is the only reading here that could have disagreed.
answerText: The sounder gives ninety metres, not one hundred and two. The two displays share one source, so their agreement is not a check. Get an independent fix before the banked water.

choices: The plot is wrong, and the sounding is right.
The sounder has failed, and the plot is right.
The chart is out of date along here.
The boat is on the plot, and the water is shallow today.
Ordinary noise in the reading, nothing more.
choiceMechanisms: Both displays repeat one source, so they cannot disagree. The bottom is a separate measurement.
One instrument has failed, and the two agreeing displays are right.
The survey is old, and the bottom has changed since it was made.
Tide and air pressure move the surface, not the bottom.
Twelve metres is inside the usual scatter of a sounding.
rebuttals: A failed sounder is the comfortable answer, and it needs the two displays to be right. They agree because they share one source.
An old chart moves the bottom, not the boat. Possible, and it explains nothing about three and a half hours with no fix.
Tide and air pressure move the surface a metre or two, not twelve. The bottom is where the bottom is.
Twelve metres is not scatter. A sounder wrong by that much would be failing in a way the trace itself would show.
text.headline: The two navigation displays agree exactly, and the bottom agrees with neither.

title: Where the sound will not go
task: Say where the contact has gone.
scene: The sound trace reads faster above sixty metres and slower below it. A contact held for forty minutes while the boat stayed at twenty. Then it vanished in one sweep, and nothing else changed.
assumes: sound travels at different speeds through warmer and colder water
sound bends toward the slower water
takeaway: Sound bends as it travels, which leaves places a listening boat cannot hear into at all.
question: The contact was held near the surface and is now gone. Where is it?
why: Sound does not travel in straight lines through the sea. It bends toward the slower water, and the water below sixty metres here is slower. Bend a path far enough and there are places the sound from our own depth never reaches. A contact that crosses into one of those does not fade away. It goes in a single sweep, while every other trace stays where it was. That suddenness is the shape of a shadow, not of distance.
answerText: It has gone under the layer, into water our sound does not reach. The clue is how fast it went — one sweep, with every other trace unchanged.

choices: Under the layer, where the sound from our depth does not reach.
Out of range, since detection fades off with distance.
Astern, into the boat's own blind sector behind the propeller.
Nowhere. It has shut down and is making no sound at all.
rebuttals: Losing something to range is gradual. This went in one sweep, which is a change in geometry rather than in distance.
The blind sector is a direction astern. This contact's direction had not moved.
Something that goes quiet fades over minutes. This one was there, and then was not.

title: What has to be true before the boat commits
task: Put the passage checks in the order they have to be done.
scene: Rask shuts the sonar-room door and lays out the checks for the passage. The narrows are on the next chart panel. Once the boat is committed there is no room to turn round.
assumes: a measurement can mean nothing without an earlier one to read it against
takeaway: A plan is ordered by what each measurement needs before it can mean anything.
why: A plan is a list of things that have to be true when the boat commits. Each one is what the next gets read against. Without the boat's own noise, a new sound is only a sound. Without the layer, a missing tone looks like an empty sea instead of a bent path. Bearings take time, so they cannot be started at the entrance. And the lost-contact rule is agreed early for a different reason. Afterwards, everybody is busy.

cards: Record what the boat itself sounds like, because nothing new can be heard as new without it.
Find the depth of the layer, because it decides which missing sounds are missing for a reason.
Hold the contacts long enough to see which way their bearings are moving.
Agree what the boat does if contact is lost, while there is still contact to lose.
rebuttals: Our own noise first. Nothing is recognised as new until you know what the boat sounds like.
The layer second, because it decides which missing sounds are missing for a reason.
Bearing movement third. It takes time, and it needs the other two before it can be read at all.
The lost-contact rule before the entrance, while there is still contact to lose and somebody free to argue.

title: The margin that survives being wrong
task: Work out how much clear water is left if the boat runs the middle.
scene: The narrows fill the next chart panel. They are four sea miles across, the bank is on the left, and the circle round our own position is two miles wide.
assumes: a plotted position is the middle of a circle of doubt, not a fact
takeaway: A route is chosen against the doubt, not against the pencil line.
question: How much clear water is left if the boat runs the middle of the channel?
why: The circle round a plotted position is the honest width of where the boat might be. So a route is planned against the circle, not against the line at its middle. The whole circle has to stay in safe water. Half the channel is two miles. Half the circle is one mile. What is left over is one mile. Four miles of channel sounds generous until the doubt is drawn at the same scale.

estimate.prompt: Four miles of channel, and a position that could be a mile out either way.
estimate.question: How much clear water is left if the boat runs the middle?
estimate.relationship: Margin = half the channel − half the width of the doubt.
estimate.explanation: Running the middle puts two miles between the plotted position and each side. The boat could be a mile off toward either. What is left over is what the route survives on.
estimate.solution: Half the channel is two miles. Half the doubt is one. The margin is one mile.

title: The one shaft speed that rings
task: Say why the hull rings at one shaft speed and nowhere else.
scene: At ninety-two turns the after compartment rings loudly enough to hear through a bulkhead. At eighty-five and at a hundred it does not. Nothing else in the plant changes.
assumes: everything has speeds at which it prefers to shake, the way a swing does
takeaway: A small push repeated in time with something's own rhythm builds a large movement.
question: The hull rings at one shaft speed and nowhere else. Why that one?
why: Everything has a rhythm it prefers to shake at, the way a swing does. Push a swing at any old moment and little happens. Push it in time and it goes higher on every push. The propeller blades hit the water a set number of times each turn. At one shaft speed that beat lands in time with the compartment's own rhythm. Either side of it, the pushes fall out of step.

choices: At that speed the blades push in time with the structure's own rhythm, so the shaking grows.
The shaft is out of balance, and being out of balance gets worse with speed.
A bearing is failing, and a failing bearing is loudest in the middle of its range.
Bubbles start coming off the blades at that speed and stop above it.
rebuttals: Being out of balance gets worse smoothly with speed, so a hundred turns would ring louder than ninety-two.
A failing bearing gets worse with speed and load. It does not pick one turn count and go quiet either side.
Bubbles off the blades increase with speed. They do not switch off above some line.

title: Under the deck plates
task: Read the flows, decide which ones belong in the sum, and close the water balance.
scene: The forward bilge alarm has gone twice, and water shows through the deck-plate slots. Machinist's Mate Ruth Hallam marks the level a minute apart while the drain pump runs. Command wants the inflow now.
assumes: a rise in the bilge is what stayed behind, not what came in
a pump that is running takes water out during the same minute
takeaway: What piles up is what came in minus what was taken out, so anything already removing has to go back into the sum.
question: How fast is water coming in, before the pump takes any of it out?
why: The rise in the bilge is only what stayed behind during that minute. The pump ran the whole time, and what it threw over the side never showed on the deck plates. So the sum is what piled up plus what was pumped. Eighty-eight and fifty-five make about a hundred and forty-three gallons a minute. The fresh-water tank and the cooling flow did not change, so they add nothing. A pump makes a bad leak look small.
answerText: About one hundred and forty-three gallons a minute. Eighty-eight piled up in the bilge, and another fifty-five went over the side through the pump in the same minute.

title: What ninety metres puts behind the valve
task: Work out how hard the sea is pushing on the fitting.
scene: The suspect hull fitting is ninety metres down. Ferro wants to know what the sea is pushing with on the far side of it, before anybody touches that valve.
assumes: water pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every ten metres of depth
takeaway: Pressure grows straight in step with depth, so depth decides how hard a leak pushes.
question: About how much pressure is the sea putting on the fitting?
why: Water is heavy, and every metre of it above the fitting presses down. About ten metres of sea adds one atmosphere, so ninety metres adds nine. Add the air we all live under and the outside of that fitting sits near ten atmospheres. That is why a small hole this deep drives so much water. It is also why shutting the hull valve matters more than fitting another pump. A pump fights the flow. The valve takes the push away.

estimate.prompt: The fitting sits ninety metres down. Water adds about one atmosphere of pressure for every ten metres.
estimate.question: About how much pressure is the sea putting on the fitting?
estimate.relationship: Pressure added = depth ÷ ten metres for each atmosphere.
estimate.explanation: This is the pressure the sea adds. The air at the surface adds one more on top, which is why the outside total is about ten.
estimate.solution: Ninety divided by ten is nine atmospheres of added pressure.

title: What else that valve feeds
task: Match each order to what it actually does.
scene: Two valves will stop the water: the one at the hull and the one inboard. The same header feeds the sonar cooling. Haruki wants each order matched to what it really does.
assumes: one pipe header can serve more than one system
takeaway: Every valve you shut takes something away from somebody, and the order decides what.
why: Shutting a valve is never free, because a pipe rarely serves one thing. Here the same header carries the leak and the cooling for the sonar array. Only the valve at the hull separates the boat from the sea, so only that one ends the flood. The inboard valve stops the flow at the break and leaves the header full. A pump buys time. Telling sonar moves no water, and it is why that watch is not caught out.

scenarios: Shut the hull valve first.
Shut only the inboard supply valve.
Start a second portable pump before isolating.
Tell sonar before the header is shut.
choices: Stops the sea at the hull, which is the only cut that ends it.
Stops flow to the break, and leaves the sea joined to the header.
Buys minutes and changes nothing about where the water comes from.
Gives that watch warning that their cooling is about to stop.
rebuttals: The hull valve is the only cut between the boat and the ocean. Everything else works on water that is already inside.
The inboard valve stops the flow at the break and leaves the header full of sea. Useful, and not the end of it.
A second pump raises the rate going out. It buys minutes and leaves the source alone.
Telling sonar moves no water at all. It gives that watch time to get ready before the cooling stops.

title: Three legs, three different actions
task: Match each leg of the fire to the action that removes it.
scene: Chief Electrician's Mate Bede Okonkwo puts the three legs of the fire on the board. The fault that keeps lighting it. The insulation that burns. The air in the compartment.
assumes: a fire needs fuel, air and something to start it
takeaway: Killing the power stops the heating and the shock. It does not put out what is already burning.
why: A live fault keeps pouring heat into insulation that is already alight. So the first move is to open the breaker and prove the cable dead. That stops the heating and the shock together. It does not stop the fire. Hot insulation burns on until something cools it. The air is then controlled, to starve the flame and steer the smoke. A hot bulkhead is a warning to watch, not a fourth thing to fight.

scenarios: The live fault that keeps re-lighting the cable.
The cable insulation that is actually burning.
The air in the compartment feeding the flame.
The heat coming through the bulkhead to the next space.
choices: Open the breaker, then prove the cable dead with a meter.
Cool it below the heat it needs to re-light.
Shut the vent to the space, so the flame stops being fed.
Set a boundary, and read it with a heat gun.
rebuttals: The live fault goes when the breaker is open and the cable is proved dead. Until then everything else fights a symptom.
The burning insulation is the fuel. Cool it below the heat it needs to light again.
The air feeding the flame is cut by shutting the vent. Down here there is nowhere to vent to.
Heat reaching the next compartment is not a leg of this fire. It is a boundary, and you read it with a heat gun.

title: What a lamp is worth
task: Put the steps in the order that proves it before anybody fights it.
scene: Smoke is pushing through the door. The switchboard lamp says the bus is open, and a meter on the cable reads four hundred and forty volts. The hose team is masked up, waiting.
assumes: a bus can be fed from more than one source
takeaway: An indicator reports what somebody believes. A meter reports what is there.
why: The lamp reports what the switchboard believes. A meter on the cable reports what the cable is doing. The two can disagree, because contacts stick, lamps fail, and another source can feed the same cable from behind. Water on a live cable carries current back into the hose team. So the order is fixed. Open the source, test the cable, prove it dead, then fight. The meter turns a belief into a fact.

cards: Open the breaker for that bus.
Meter the cable in the compartment and prove it dead.
Go in on air masks and fight the fire.
Set boundaries and read them until the seat is cold.
Bring the loads back on, the vital ones first.
rebuttals: Open the breaker first. Nothing downstream is safe to touch while the source is still joined to it.
Meter the cable second, in the compartment. This is the step the lamp cannot do for you, and it is the one that got skipped.
Go in third, on air, once the cable is proved dead.
Read the boundaries until the seat is cold, and bring the loads back in order. A fire called out early is a fire you fight twice.

title: Smoke is not only a breathing problem
task: Say what the smoke has done to the way this is fought.
scene: You cannot see half a metre. The far bulkhead is eight metres away. Head height reads sixty degrees against twenty-eight at the deck. The fire is behind a panel where nobody can see it.
assumes: a fire inside a structure does not show you where it is
takeaway: Smoke takes away the instrument you were using most, which is your own eyes.
question: What does the smoke change about how this casualty is fought?
why: Smoke does more than make breathing hard. It takes sight away, so a team can lose the route, the boundary and each other within a few metres. Sixty degrees at head height against twenty-eight at the deck also says the heat is stacked in layers. Things can get much worse above that layer while the floor still feels survivable. Masks fix the breathing and nothing else. From here the space has to be measured rather than looked at.

choices: The space cannot be read by eye any more, so the boundaries have to be measured instead.
Nothing, as long as everybody is on air.
The fire will put itself out once the smoke pushes the air out.
The compartment has to be given up until the smoke clears.
rebuttals: Masks keep the team working. They do not give back the information the smoke took away.
A fire eating the air also makes carbon monoxide, which is worse rather than self-solving.
Giving up the compartment hands it to the fire, and somebody still has to read the boundaries.

title: The compartment the scrubber cannot reach
task: Say which explanation accounts for every reading.
scene: The scrubber is running and its outlet reads clean. A handheld meter in berthing reads far higher than the sensor fitted there. Control and machinery read normal on handhelds.
assumes: a machine can only clean the air that reaches it
takeaway: Which compartments a plant is really treating is decided by where the air goes.
question: Which explanation accounts for every reading here?
why: A scrubber can only clean air that reaches it. Shut one damper and a compartment drops out of the loop while the plant's own outlet still reads clean. Here the handheld in berthing agrees with how the people in there feel, and handhelds elsewhere read normal. So the problem is in one space. The sensor fitted in that space disagrees with both, which makes it a second fault. Two faults at once is allowed. The evidence decides, not tidiness.

choices: Berthing is shut out of the air loop, and its fitted sensor is wrong as well.
The whole boat's air is going bad.
The scrubber has stopped taking carbon dioxide out.
The handheld meter is reading high by mistake.
Ordinary background, nothing more.
choiceMechanisms: A shut damper cuts the space out of the loop, and a bad fitted sensor hides the rise.
A boat-wide failure would lift the readings in several compartments at once.
A failed scrubber would show at its own outlet, and everywhere else too.
A bad handheld would not explain the shut damper or how people in there feel.
Air going bad in one space, with two instruments disagreeing, is not background.
rebuttals: Control and machinery read normal on their own handhelds, so this is not boat-wide.
The scrubber's own outlet reads clean, which says the plant is doing its job.
The shut damper and the symptoms in berthing both point at something real in that space.
One space going bad while two instruments disagree is not ordinary noise.
text.headline: Berthing reads high on a handheld and normal on its own sensor, and the plant says it is fine.

title: Nine people and a shut damper
task: Turn the rate the air is going bad into a deadline.
scene: Nine people sleep in a space with the damper shut. The corpsman, Elena Navarro, wants to know how long that air has left.
assumes: a person breathes out carbon dioxide steadily, hour after hour
takeaway: A rate turns a limit into a deadline.
question: How long until the carbon dioxide in there rises by one per cent?
why: Anything arriving at a steady rate piles up in step with time. One per cent of that space is three hundred and sixty litres of carbon dioxide. Nine people put out about one hundred and eighty litres between them every hour. Three hundred and sixty divided by one hundred and eighty is two hours. It is a rough number, and it does what the word stuffy cannot. It gives the corpsman a time to work against.

estimate.prompt: One per cent of the air in that space is three hundred and sixty litres. Each person breathes out about twenty litres of carbon dioxide an hour, and there are nine of them.
estimate.question: How long until the carbon dioxide in there rises by one per cent?
estimate.relationship: Time = the amount you can allow ÷ the rate it arrives at.
estimate.explanation: The rate is nine people together, not one. Divide by one person's rate and the answer comes out nine times too long, which is a deadline nobody could use.
estimate.solution: Three hundred and sixty ÷ (twenty × nine) is two hours.
labels: 360 litres (one per cent of the air in here)
20 litres an hour (each person breathes out)
36 cubic metres (the air in the space)

title: What one fan takes with it
task: Say what one shared fan means for the air plan.
scene: The drawing shows one fan feeding the scrubber and the after spaces through the same trunk. The watch bill lists them as two systems, and the air plan counts on both.
assumes: a system is only as separate as the parts it does not share
takeaway: Two systems sharing one part are one system as soon as that part fails.
question: One fan feeds the scrubber and the after spaces. What does that mean for the plan?
why: One fan can do two jobs and still be one failure. If the scrubber and the after spaces share that fan and that trunk, losing it takes both away at once. Writing them in two boxes on the watch bill does not make them separate. Separate means a different fan, a different supply, or a different route. Until one of those exists, the air plan has a single failure that reaches several spaces.

choices: The fan is a single point of failure, and the plan needs another path or a stated fallback.
Nothing. Two systems on one fan is normal, and the fan is reliable.
Run the scrubber harder, so a fan failure leaves more room.
Seal off the after spaces, since they are downstream.
rebuttals: Reliable is not separate. A reliable shared part still takes both systems with it when it does go.
Running the scrubber harder uses more of the same air path, and shortens the time you have.
Sealing the after spaces removes them from the plan instead of protecting them, and people sleep there.

title: Four casualties, one crew
task: Decide which one gets the first team.
scene: Four reports hit control almost together. Water forward. A bus lost aft. The plot gone soft. A crewman down with a broken wrist. Every team leader is waiting for the first move.
assumes: some problems get worse on their own, and some do not
takeaway: Order casualties by how fast they get worse, not by how loud they are.
question: What gets the first team?
why: Triage sorts by speed, and by what cannot be undone. It does not sort by what sounds worst. Water coming in takes away the thing holding the boat up, and it spreads into new spaces. A lost bus has already done its damage. A soft plot gets worse with every mile toward shallow water, and slowing down freezes it. A broken wrist hurts and stays the same size for an hour. The first team goes where waiting costs the most.

choices: The flooding, because it is the only one getting worse by itself.
The injured crewman, because a person comes before equipment.
The lost bus, because everything else runs on power.
The plot, because the boat is still heading for a bank.
rebuttals: The injured man matters and he is stable. A broken wrist is treated and cleared, and it is not growing while you decide.
The bus is already lost. Everything downstream of it failed minutes ago, and none of it gets worse while the team goes forward.
The plot does get worse every minute, and slowing the boat freezes it. That is a decision, not a team.

title: Who does the things you are not doing
task: Keep the one thing that cannot wait, and hand over the rest with an owner, a first move and a number.
scene: The flooding is losing now: the pump moves sixty litres a minute against forty coming in. A fire boundary aft is heating. The air is steady, and a crewman has a broken wrist.
assumes: how fast a problem is changing matters as much as how big it is
a real handover names an owner, a first move and when to report back
takeaway: A handover is finished when somebody knows what to do first and when to come back.
question: Which problem do you keep, and what does each of the others get?
why: The fire boundary is the one thing here that gets worse fast enough to cross a line while you are still talking. Fifty-four degrees, climbing six a minute, and the limit is eighty. That is minutes away. The flooding is already losing twenty litres a minute, so it can be watched. The air and the wrist are steady. Everything you hand over needs an owner, a first move and a number that brings it back to you.
answerText: Keep the heating boundary yourself. Hand over the falling bilge, the steady air and the broken wrist. Each one gets a first move and a number that brings it back.

title: Slowing down as a decision
task: Work out how much thinking time slowing down buys.
scene: The plot is still being rebuilt. The boat makes eight knots toward a bank nine miles ahead. Lieutenant Commander Theo Whitfield asks what coming down to three knots buys.
assumes: distance divided by speed is time
takeaway: Slowing down turns a distance problem into a time budget.
question: How much more time does coming down to three knots buy?
why: Time is the only thing in a casualty you can make more of, and speed is the price. Nine miles at eight knots is a little over an hour. The same nine miles at three knots is three hours. Slowing costs progress and buys everything else. The plot gets rebuilt. The flood gets fought. The passage is still there afterwards. Work out what eight knots is spending, in minutes, before deciding the boat can afford it.

estimate.prompt: Nine miles to the bank at eight knots, with the option of coming down to three.
estimate.question: How much more time does coming down to three knots buy?
estimate.relationship: Time = distance ÷ speed. The gain is the slow time minus the fast time.
estimate.explanation: An hour is not enough time to fight a flood and rebuild a plot. Three hours is. Speed is the one number on this list you control.
estimate.solution: Nine ÷ eight is about 1.1 hours. Nine ÷ three is three hours. Slowing buys nearly two more.

title: From the sea to the bearing
task: Build the heat path in order, then name the link that is holding it up.
scene: The bearing is running warm at its usual load. Haruki puts the cooling diagram on the table before anybody touches a valve. Six stages, from the bearing to the sea.
assumes: heat has to be handed on through every link before it can leave the boat
the hottest part is not automatically the broken one
takeaway: A chain of handovers is limited by its weakest required link, not by its hottest part.
question: Where does the heat travel, and which handover is holding it up?
why: The bearing makes the heat, and that does not make the bearing the fault. The heat has to move into the oil, across the oil cooler, into the fresh water, across the sea cooler, and out. Weaken any one of those handovers and everything behind it gets hotter. The readings show normal load and low seawater flow. So the last step out is the one holding it up. Writing the chain first stops the hottest part taking the blame.
answerText: Bearing, oil, oil cooler, fresh water, sea cooler, overboard. The weak link is the seawater flow at the end, not the hot bearing at the start.

title: One link is not handing the heat on
task: Say which link in the chain has failed.
scene: The oil and the fresh water are both hot. Seawater goes into the cooler at nine degrees and comes out at twenty-three, against a normal twelve. The flow gauge reads forty-five per cent.
assumes: a cooler needs water moving on both sides to shift heat
takeaway: Less water carrying the same heat has to come out hotter.
question: Which link in the chain has failed?
why: How much heat water carries away depends on how much water there is, and on how much it warms up. Keep the heat the same and halve the water, and every litre carries twice as much. So it comes out hotter. Here the sea water warms fourteen degrees instead of three, with the flow at forty-five per cent. The hot fresh water says the heat reaches the cooler. The big rise says too little water is taking it away.
answerText: Too little seawater is going through the cooler. The heat gets that far and then has nothing to leave in.

choices: Not enough seawater going through the cooler.
The oil cooler is furred up.
The bearing has started making far more heat.
The oil temperature sensor is faulty.
Ordinary background, nothing more.
choiceMechanisms: Less water carrying the same heat has to come out hotter.
A furred oil cooler would leave the fresh water cool, not hot.
More heat would warm everything, and it would not explain a flow gauge at forty-five per cent.
One bad sensor cannot make the fresh water hot and the seawater warm as well.
A fourteen-degree rise at forty-five per cent flow is not normal at this load.
rebuttals: The fresh water is hot, so heat is crossing the oil cooler into it.
The gauge reading forty-five per cent points straight at the flow, further down the chain.
Several temperatures moved together, so one bad oil sensor cannot cover it.
A fourteen-degree rise with the flow that low is well outside the normal pattern.
text.headline: The oil is hot, the fresh water is hot, and the seawater leaves far warmer than it arrived.

title: The breaker nobody logged
task: Say what the open breaker tells you about the quiet lineup.
scene: The second seawater pump did not trip. Its breaker is open at the switchboard. The quiet lineup from two watches ago is still in force, and nobody wrote down what it turned off.
assumes: a watch hands over to people who were not there
takeaway: A setting nobody wrote down is a setting nobody puts back.
question: What does this tell you about the quiet lineup?
why: The quiet lineup was a deliberate trade, and the reason behind it did not survive the watch change. A log has to carry more than the fact that a machine was shut down. It has to say what that machine was cooling, and when it should come back. Without that, the next watch sees an open breaker and cannot tell a plan from a fault. So this cooling problem is really a handover problem.

choices: Turning a machine off needs a record of what it was cooling.
The quiet lineup should undo itself once the passage ends.
The bearing should have an alarm that starts the pump again.
Nothing. The watch that shut it made a fair trade at the time.
rebuttals: Quiet running is a fair reason to shut a pump down. The fault is in the handover, not the decision.
A pump that restarts itself would undo the point of a deliberately quiet boat.
It was fair at the time and stopped being fair an hour later, which is the whole problem.

title: Five small problems
task: Say which one has to change first.
scene: Nothing on the board is red. The plot is four hours old. The contact is faint. The forward bilge is wet, one scrubber is down, and a bearing is warm. The narrows are still ahead.
assumes: how fast something is changing matters more than whether it looks odd
takeaway: A pile of small problems can be worse than one big one, because none of them shouts.
question: What is the first thing that has to change?
why: Five small problems are not equally urgent, because they do not change at the same speed. The old plot gets more dangerous with every mile toward the narrows. The faint contact needs time before it means anything. A wet bilge matters when the level moves. A scrubber down is a deadline only if the air is rising. A warm bearing matters if it is climbing. Deal first with the one growing fastest, and give the rest owners and numbers.

choices: How old the position is
The contact nobody has resolved
The wet bilge
The carbon dioxide
The warm bearing
choiceMechanisms: Everything else is steady and measured. The plot is the only one getting worse on its own, and the passage runs on it.
A faint contact that may be nothing, and can be watched while something else is fixed.
Water that is not rising, which is a note in the log rather than a casualty.
A slow rise with twenty hours of room behind it.
A steady temperature, which is a watch item rather than a fault.
rebuttals: The contact may be nothing, and it can be held and watched while something else gets fixed.
A wet bilge that is not rising is a note in the log. It becomes a casualty when the level moves.
Carbon dioxide rising slowly has twenty hours of room behind it, and it is measured all the time.
A bearing sitting at sixty-eight degrees is a watch item. Steady is the word that matters.
text.headline: Nothing on the board is red, and the boat is an hour from a passage it cannot take twice.

title: Everything you are not doing yourself
task: Match each open problem to the order that fits it.
scene: You keep the soft plot yourself, and four other things are open. Whitfield stands by the watch bill with names ready and nobody assigned. This is the last watch of the patrol.
assumes: an instruction has to be something the person receiving it can act on alone
takeaway: An order with a number in it can be acted on alone. Watch it cannot.
why: A useful order lets somebody act without guessing what you meant. It names who owns it, what to do first, and what brings them back to you. Log the bilge and report a change. Hold the contact until its bearing moves. Restore the scrubber, or name the hour. Get the pump back and say what it costs in noise. Watch it sounds responsible, gives nobody a decision, and leaves every problem attached to you.

scenarios: The forward bilge, wet and not rising.
The faint contact nobody has resolved.
The scrubber that is down.
The bearing running warm.
choices: Log the level every ten minutes, and report a change rather than a number.
Hold it until the bearing moves, and report before it is certain.
Get it running, or name the hour when the air stops being optional.
Get the second cooling pump back, and say what that costs in noise.
rebuttals: A bilge that is wet and not rising needs a level every ten minutes and a change reported. A change, because the number alone means nothing.
An unresolved contact needs holding until its bearing moves, and a report before it is certain. Waiting for certainty wastes the geometry.
A scrubber that is down needs restoring, or an hour named when the air stops being optional. That hour is what command plans around.
A warm bearing needs the second pump back, and the noise cost said out loud, because that cost is why it was shut down.

title: Why the level pulses three times a second
task: Work out how fast the loudness swells from the two tones.
scene: Two tones sit at one hundred and forty-seven and one hundred and fifty hertz, on the same bearing. The sound swells and fades in a steady rhythm while both tones hold still.
assumes: two sounds arriving together add up, and can also cancel
hertz means how many times a second something repeats
takeaway: Two close tones together make the loudness rise and fall at the difference between them.
question: How many swells a second should those two tones make?
why: Two tones close together take turns lining up and cancelling. When their crests arrive together the sound is loud. A moment later one has slipped behind, they work against each other, and the sound drops away. How fast that cycle repeats is only the difference between the two pitches. One hundred and fifty against one hundred and forty-seven gives three swells a second. Neither tone has moved at all.
answerText: Three swells a second, which is the difference between the two tones. Neither tone has changed pitch.

choices: Two sources beating together, at the difference between their pitches.
One source whose speed is changing three times a second.
A fault in the display, since two steady tones cannot pulse.
Our own machinery, folded into the band.
rebuttals: A change in speed moves a tone up or down. It does not make the loudness swell on a fixed beat.
Two steady tones pulsing is exactly what adding waves sounds like. The display shows the tones, not the sum.
Our own machinery would show on every bearing. These two are on one.

estimate.prompt: Two tones, at one hundred and forty-seven and one hundred and fifty hertz, in water where sound travels about fifteen hundred metres a second.
estimate.question: How many swells a second do the two tones make?
estimate.relationship: Swells each second = the difference between the two pitches.
estimate.explanation: Only the two pitches set the beat. The speed of sound matters for working out a wavelength, and not for this subtraction.
estimate.solution: One hundred and fifty take away one hundred and forty-seven is three swells a second.
labels: 1,500 metres a second (the speed of sound in water)
